scenes.heading: narratr

steps.label: Document
steps.cue: You point it at a document

scenes.narration: Narrator turns a document into a narrated video, and it runs entirely on your own machine. You point it at a document, it writes the script, and your laptop does the rest while you get on with something else.

scenes.heading: The usual failure
scenes.narration: Every project like this fails the same way. You build the slides first, then try to make the narration fit them. The timing drifts, and there is no fixing it, because every edit breaks the alignment all over again.

scenes.heading: Narration is the clock
scenes.narration: So invert it. The script comes first. Speech renders each scene and reports exactly how long it turned out to be. Only then does anything get drawn, and the renderer is simply told how much time it has. Synchronisation stops being a problem you solve.

scenes.heading: End to end
scenes.narration: A document goes in and becomes a scene list. Each scene is narrated and measured. The visuals are drawn to fit the time the narration takes. Then the pieces are joined into one file.

scenes.heading: Zero dollars

cards.title: Twice the runtime
cards.detail: A 2 min clip costs about 4 min
cards.cue: What you pay instead is time

scenes.narration: A video costs nothing to make. There is no subscription to buy and no monthly floor to clear. What you pay instead is time, at roughly twice the length of the finished video. A two minute clip takes about four minutes, and none of it needs you watching.

scenes.heading: Where it stands
scenes.narration: As things stand, the whole pipeline works. Runs checkpoint after every scene, so a closed laptop lid costs you ninety seconds rather than the afternoon. And because everything is cached by content, editing one slide costs seconds rather than a rebuild.
